items.label: Concavity
items.note: A sign change is what matters for inflection.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.md: Use $f^\prime$ for rising and falling, and $f^{\prime\prime}$ for bending. Do not call a discontinuity an inflection point. An even-multiplicity root may preserve the sign.

blocks.title: Written exam practice
blocks.md: On a full sketch question, show both charts and label extrema and inflection coordinates. On a graph of $f^\prime$, height gives the sign of $f^\prime$ and slope gives the sign of $f^{\prime\prime}$.

blocks.title: Curve sketching with derivatives
blocks.focus: Track how the first derivative and second derivative answer different questions.

steps.title: First chart
steps.why: Classify extrema by changes in monotonicity.

steps.title: Second chart
steps.md: $f^{\prime\prime}=6(x-1)$ switches from negative to positive at 1.
steps.why: This determines bending independently of rising and falling.

steps.title: Anchor the graph
steps.md: $f=x^2(x-3)$ vanishes at 0 and 3. Plot the three key points and draw the cubic ends.
steps.why: The intercept and end behavior constrain the shape.

blocks.title: A stationary point without an extremum

steps.title: Test the first derivative
steps.why: No sign change means no local extremum.

steps.title: Test the second derivative
steps.why: The function is continuous, so this is an inflection.

blocks.title: Recall without notes
cards: Local maximum at a continuous join.
What if the second derivative test gives zero?
Use the first derivative sign chart.
Can a graph fall and be concave up?
Yes. Its negative slopes can become less negative.
